question: How does the principal waltz carry a long melody across its three-beat accompaniment?
intro: Stokowski’s Philadelphia recording was made in Camden in 1934 and released that year. This first side includes the introduction and early waltz; the comparison aligns only the shared principal-waltz passage, not the unequal introductions or side endings.

cues.title: A Camden recording
cues.text: The source places the Philadelphia Orchestra and Stokowski in Camden’s Church Studio No. 2 in 1934. It identifies this file as part 1 of the Waltz of the Flowers.
cues.evidence: Commons gives the studio, first recording and release dates and side designation.

cues.title: The dance gathers shape
cues.text: After the quieter introductory region, the principal waltz takes shape. Compare the sustained melody with the regular accompaniment, not the different lengths of the three introductions.
cues.evidence: The strongest report boundary is 0:54, followed by rising relative level through 1:00. The waltz’s formal role is documented in the existing score-informed reference notes.

cues.title: A fuller answering span
cues.text: This part of the early waltz gains recorded weight. Listen for the longer phrase above the accompaniment as you switch between orchestra and band.
cues.evidence: A 1:24 boundary precedes a rise from −18.9 dB at 1:20 to −12.0 at 1:25 and −10.8 at 1:30. The map covers this common passage.

cues.title: The side continues alone
cues.text: A later crest lies beyond the shared comparison window. The stream still contains the rest of this record side, but it is not a complete waltz and is not used for a whole-work duration comparison.
cues.evidence: The highest relative-level window is 2:25 at −8.0 dB. The comparison ends at reference 140 seconds; Commons identifies part 1 only.

composer.epithet: He used the timing of dance and theatre to make a symphony’s return, interruption or collapse physically audible.
facts: Imperial School of Jurisprudence; Saint Petersburg Conservatory, 1862–65, with Anton Rubinstein and Nikolai Zaremba
Nadezhda von Meck supplied an allowance from 1877 to 1890; their correspondence became a major record of his working life
Six numbered symphonies and Manfred; three ballets; operas, concertos, chamber music, piano music and songs
composer.background:
Tchaikovsky was born at Votkinsk, where his father managed an ironworks. Music belonged to the household before it became a profession: his governess Fanny Dürbach remembered the child’s intense responses to it, and he began piano lessons early. His formal training nevertheless pointed towards government service. In 1850 he entered the preparatory class of the Imperial School of Jurisprudence in Saint Petersburg, separated from his family. His mother died of cholera in 1854. After graduating in 1859 he worked in the Ministry of Justice, while concerts, opera and lessons gradually occupied more of his time.

When Anton Rubinstein’s Saint Petersburg Conservatory opened in 1862, Tchaikovsky joined its first generation of students. He studied composition with Rubinstein and theoretical subjects with Nikolai Zaremba, leaving government employment in 1863. The training mattered practically: he could organise large forms, prepare orchestral scores and teach harmony. In 1866 Nikolai Rubinstein recruited him for the new Moscow Conservatory. Tchaikovsky taught there until 1878, wrote criticism and translated pedagogical material. His early reputation grew through this sustained professional work.
